name: 24LC64T-I_SN
title: 24AA64/24LC64: 64 Kbit I2C serial EEPROM
summary: A 64 Kbit (8192 x 8) electrically erasable PROM on a two-wire I2C-compatible bus, organized as eight blocks of 8 Kbit. The 24AA64 runs from 1.8 V and the 24LC64 from 2.5 V, both up to 5.5 V and 400 kHz (the 24AA64 at 100 kHz below 2.5 V). Writes go through a 32-byte page buffer with a self-timed erase-and-write cycle; three address pins put up to eight devices on one bus, and a WP pin locks the whole array against writes. 24LC64T-I/SN is the 2.5 V part, industrial temperature, in the 150 mil SOIC on tape and reel.
key_figures: 400 kHz at 2.5 V to 5.5 V; 100 kHz at 1.8 V to 2.5 V (24AA64)
5 ms max (byte or page); 2 ms typical for a page write
3 mA max write, 1 mA max read at VCC = 5.5 V, 400 kHz
1 µA max industrial, 5 µA max automotive

notes: An order code is the device, a temperature letter and a package code: 24LC64T-I/SN is the 2.5 V device on tape and reel, industrial range, 150 mil SOIC.
Temperature codes: I = -40 °C to +85 °C, E = -40 °C to +125 °C. The 24AA64 is offered in the I range only.
Package codes: P = 8-lead plastic DIP, 300 mil body; SN = 8-lead plastic SOIC, 150 mil body; SM = 8-lead plastic SOIC, 208 mil body; ST = 8-lead plastic TSSOP, 4.4 mm; MS = 8-lead plastic MSOP.
The X parts have the rotated pinout and come in TSSOP (ST) only.
The T suffix is tape and reel. Factory programming (QTP) is offered.

operation.text: The device is always a slave on the two-wire bus. The master drives SCL, decides when the bus is used and issues START and STOP; either side may send or receive data, by the master's choice.

Idle: SDA and SCL both high. START: SDA falls while SCL is high; every command begins with one. STOP: SDA rises while SCL is high; every operation ends with one. A transfer starts only on an idle bus. Otherwise SDA must hold steady while SCL is high and change only while SCL is low, one clock per bit.

The receiver of each byte answers with an acknowledge on a ninth clock that the master supplies, holding SDA low through the high phase of that clock with setup and hold times met. During a read the master marks the last byte by leaving it unacknowledged; the device then releases SDA high so the master can send STOP. While an internal write cycle runs the device acknowledges nothing.

The first byte after START is the control byte: the code 1010, then chip-select bits A2, A1, A0, then R/W (1 = read, 0 = write). The device answers only when the chip-select bits match the levels on its A2, A1 and A0 pins, so up to eight devices share one bus.
Two address bytes follow a write control byte, high byte first. Only A12 to A0 are used; the top three bits of the high byte are don't-care.

With eight devices on a bus, software can use control-byte bits A0, A1 and A2 as address bits A13, A14 and A15 for a contiguous 512 Kbit space. A sequential read does not continue from one device into the next.

START, a write control byte, the high then low address bytes and one data byte, each acknowledged by the device, then STOP. The STOP starts the internal write cycle. Afterwards the address counter points at the next location.

As a byte write, but the master keeps sending up to 31 more data bytes before STOP; they collect in the 32-byte page buffer and are written together after STOP. Each byte advances only the low five bits of the address pointer, so more than 32 bytes wrap and overwrite the first ones received. Pages begin at multiples of 32; a page write that runs past the end of its page wraps to that page's start and overwrites it, so software must keep page writes inside one page.

With WP at VCC the whole array (0000-1FFF) is protected: a write command is acknowledged but nothing is written and the device is ready for the next command at once. With WP at VSS or floating (an internal pull-down holds it low) writes proceed. WP is sampled at each write's STOP; changing it after that STOP does not affect the cycle under way. Reads are never blocked.

Because the device stays silent during its write cycle, the master can find the end of the cycle by sending START and a write control byte (R/W = 0) right after the STOP that began it. No acknowledge: still busy, send START and the control byte again. Acknowledge: the cycle is over and the next read or write can go ahead.
An internal counter keeps the address of the last byte accessed plus one. A read control byte alone returns the byte at that address; the master gives no acknowledge and sends STOP.

Set the address with a write control byte and the two address bytes, then send a new START (no STOP) and a read control byte. The device returns the addressed byte; the master leaves it unacknowledged and sends STOP. The counter then points at the following location.

Starts like a current-address or random read, but the master acknowledges each byte received and the device sends the next one, so the whole memory can be read in one operation. The pointer rolls over from 1FFF to 0000. The master ends by not acknowledging the last byte and sending STOP.
A0, A1 and A2 are compared with the chip-select bits of the control byte; they must be tied to VCC or VSS.
SDA is open drain and needs a pull-up resistor to VCC: typically 10 kΩ for 100 kHz and 2 kΩ for 400 kHz.
Writes are self-timed and include the erase. A page write typically takes 2 ms; TWC is 5 ms maximum for a byte or a page.
Inputs have Schmitt triggers for noise rejection, and the output edge rate is controlled to limit ground bounce. The device can be used as a serial ROM.
